subject: Social & Citizenship Studies
content: International relations is how countries interact through diplomacy, trade, treaties, and international organizations. Nigeria's foreign policy: Africa-centered (support for African unity, decolonization, anti-apartheid, conflict resolution), non-alignment (not taking sides in Cold War), peaceful coexistence (respect for other nations' sovereignty), economic diplomacy (attract investment, promote trade). Bilateral relations: Nigeria-UK (colonial history, economic ties, diaspora), Nigeria-US (trade, security cooperation, cultural exchange), Nigeria-China (infrastructure loans, trade, Belt and Road Initiative), Nigeria-South Africa (rivalry and cooperation, largest economies in Africa). Multilateral organizations: United Nations (UN), African Union (AU), Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), Commonwealth, Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC), OPEC. Nigerian diplomats negotiate trade deals, represent Nigerian interests, promote peace. International relations careers: diplomat, international lawyer, NGO worker, trade specialist, UN official.
summary: International relations: how countries interact. Nigeria's foreign policy: Africa-centered, non-alignment, economic diplomacy. Key partners: UK, US, China, South Africa. Organizations: UN, AU, ECOWAS.

subject: Social & Citizenship Studies
content: Development economics studies how countries improve living standards, reduce poverty, and achieve sustainable growth. Indicators: GDP per capita (average income), life expectancy (health), literacy rate (education), poverty rate (percentage below poverty line), infant mortality, access to clean water, electricity, internet. Nigeria's development challenges: poverty (over 40% below poverty line), inequality (rich-poor gap), unemployment (especially youth), infrastructure deficits (roads, electricity, internet), corruption, education quality, healthcare access. Development strategies: economic diversification (reduce oil dependence), invest in education and healthcare, improve infrastructure (roads, power, digital), fight corruption (EFCC, ICPC), attract foreign investment, promote agriculture, support small businesses. Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): 17 goals for 2030 including no poverty, zero hunger, quality education, clean water, decent work, reduced inequalities, climate action. Nigeria's development requires government policy, private sector, civil society, and citizen participation.
summary: Development economics: improving living standards. Indicators: GDP, life expectancy, literacy, poverty. Nigeria challenges: poverty, inequality, infrastructure. Strategies: diversify, invest in education/health, fight corruption.

quiz_questions.question: True or False: Development economics only focuses on money.
quiz_questions.explanation: It includes health, education, environment, and quality of life.

subject: Social & Citizenship Studies
content: Environmental policy addresses pollution, resource depletion, climate change, and conservation. Nigerian environmental issues: oil pollution (Niger Delta spills, gas flaring), deforestation (logging, farming expansion), desertification (northern states losing farmland), erosion (southeastern gully erosion), flooding (coastal and riverine areas), waste management (plastic pollution, improper disposal). Environmental laws: National Environmental Standards and Regulations Enforcement Agency (NESREA) Act, Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Act, National Oil Spill Detection and Response Agency (NOSDRA) Act, Climate Change Act (2021). Policies: National Climate Change Policy, National Afforestation Programme, Great Green Wall (combat desertification), ban on single-use plastics (some states), renewable energy incentives. Citizen actions: reduce waste (reuse, recycle), save energy (turn off lights), plant trees, report pollution, support conservation groups (NCF, NESREA). Environmental policy protects resources for future generations.
summary: Environmental policy addresses pollution, deforestation, desertification, erosion, flooding. Laws: NESREA Act, EIA Act, Climate Change Act. Citizen actions: reduce waste, plant trees, save energy.

subject: Social & Citizenship Studies
content: Civic engagement is participating in community and political life to improve conditions. Forms: voting (choosing leaders), volunteering (helping without pay), advocacy (speaking for causes), community organizing (working with neighbors), attending public meetings, contacting officials, protesting peacefully, serving on committees, joining civic organizations (Red Cross, Rotary, Lions Club, Junior Chamber International). Nigerian civic engagement examples: #EndSARS protests (youth demanding police reform), voter registration drives, community development associations (CDAs), town hall meetings, parent-teacher associations (PTA), neighborhood watch, environmental clean-ups. Civic engagement benefits: solves problems, builds community, influences policy, develops leadership skills, creates belonging. You can engage: join a school club, volunteer at local charity, attend community meetings, start a petition, write to officials, vote when eligible (18+). Democracy requires active citizens, not just voters.
summary: Civic engagement = participating in community and political life. Forms: voting, volunteering, advocacy, organizing, attending meetings, protesting. Benefits: solve problems, influence policy, build skills.

quiz_questions.question: What is a Community Development Association (CDA)?

quiz_questions.explanation: Students can volunteer, join clubs, advocate for issues.
